# Database Triggers

Procedural code the database runs on your behalf when a table changes. Triggers enforce the
cross-table and cross-row invariants that `CHECK` and foreign keys cannot reach — see
[[referential-integrity]] — and every one of their difficulties comes from the fact that they execute
*inside* the statement that fired them.

## The four kinds, and what each is for

| Kind | Fires | Can see |
|---|---|---|
| **Row-level** (`FOR EACH ROW`) | once per affected row | `:OLD` and `:NEW` for that row; **not** the table it fires on |
| **Statement-level** | once per statement | the table, but no per-row values |
| **Compound** | at up to four timing points in one object | both, with state declared once and reinitialised per statement |
| **Autonomous** (`PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION`) | as above, in its own transaction | commits independently of the caller |

## The mutating-table restriction

A row-level trigger may not query or modify the table it fires on. Oracle raises ORA-04091, because
the table is mid-change and any read would see an undefined state. Every trigger in
[[oracle-database-laboratories]] is built to stay clear of it, and the comments say how.

The cleanest example is band numbering. The naive implementation reads `MAX(band_no) + 1` from the
table it is inserting into — which is both illegal and wrong:

> "A sequence, not SELECT MAX(band_no) + 1. Reading Bands from a row-level trigger on Bands is the
> textbook mutating-table error, and MAX + 1 is also wrong under concurrency: two sessions inserting
> at once would compute the same number."
> — Oracle-Database-Laboratories/sql/03_plsql/04_triggers.sql, 2026-07-25

Two independent objections to the same line. A sequence is transactional and never touches the table,
so it answers both at once.

## State that spans a statement

Some rules need the value of something read **once before any row changed** plus totals accumulated
**across all rows** — a per-row trigger cannot hold either. Historically the workaround is three
triggers sharing package variables: `BEFORE STATEMENT` initialises, `BEFORE EACH ROW` accumulates,
`AFTER STATEMENT` settles up.

That version is implemented, kept in the tree, and labelled inferior:

> "This works, but it is fragile in a way worth naming ... The guard flag below is what stops that
> recursion. Version (b) has no such problem and is the one to prefer."
> — Oracle-Database-Laboratories/sql/03_plsql/04_triggers.sql, 2026-07-25

The fragility is re-entrancy: the `AFTER STATEMENT` trigger updates the very column its own
`BEFORE UPDATE OF` trigger watches, so it fires itself, and only a hand-managed boolean flag stops the
recursion. A **compound trigger** holds the same state in its own declaration section, reinitialised
per statement automatically, with no package globals leaking between statements. Recorded as
[[compound-trigger-over-package-state]]; both versions retained side by side per
[[keep-the-superseded-version-in-tree]] and [[multiple-solutions-side-by-side]].

## Autonomous transactions — audit that survives a rollback

Two triggers here declare `PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION` so their log write commits independently of
the transaction being audited. That is exactly what you want for "record that someone attempted this"
— the attempt happened even though the change was rejected. It is exactly what you do **not** want for
anything the caller's transaction should be able to undo, and the pragma gives no warning either way.

The validation trigger pairs it with `RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR`: log the attempt in the autonomous
transaction, commit that, then raise so the offending statement fails. Two outcomes from one trigger,
which is only possible because the two live in different transactions.

## Three naming hazards the file records

- **No reserved words as column names.** `when` and `for` read naturally for an audit table and
  neither can be used unquoted.
- **`INTO` targets named apart from the columns they read.** Naming them alike makes PL/SQL resolve
  the `WHERE` clause against the variables, matching nothing — the same collision as in
  [[plsql-exception-handling]].
- **`RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR` takes -20000 to -20999.** Any other code raises ORA-21000 in place of
  the intended message.

`ORA_LOGIN_USER` gives the session user inside a trigger; outside one it is
`SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV','SESSION_USER')`. And the insert-or-update in the audit path is a single
`MERGE` rather than a count followed by a branch, closing the race between checking and writing.
